title: Ten minutes of learning
hookLine: a fixed daily time for study, however short (Avot 1:15)
tomorrow: Isaac walked out into a field at dusk. to do what, exactly?

lines: A CALENDAR FILLS FROM THE OUTSIDE IN.
cards: A calendar fills up from the outside in: other people's meetings, practices, appointments, and whatever's left over is yours, if anything is. The Talmud has a surprising worry about that.
In its picture of the end of a life, when a person stands to give an account, the questions are practical. One of them is about your calendar. It doesn't ask how much you knew.
It asks whether you set a time. Why would that be the question?

teach.h: DID YOU FIX TIMES FOR TORAH?
teach.b: The sage Rava lists the questions a person is asked. Did you deal honestly in business? Did you fix times for Torah?
Not how much you learned, or how clever you got. Whether you fixed the time. The word is kavata, from keva, something fixed and set.

teach.h: KEVA: MAKE IT A FIXED THING.
teach.b: It echoes Shammai in Pirkei Avot: make your study a fixed thing.

Hillel, his well-known partner in argument, says why it matters: don't say, when I have free time I'll study, because maybe you'll never have free time. Anyone who has waited for a free afternoon knows how that goes.
A fixed time doesn't wait for the mood or an empty calendar. It's an appointment, and you show up on the thin days too. So how long does it have to be?
The Talmud records a generous answer.

One sage says a chapter in the morning and a chapter in the evening keeps the verse, "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth." Another goes further: even the Shema, said morning and evening, counts.
So a tradition with long nights of study also leaves the door open to ten minutes. The size can be small.
The time has to be real. Something to tell a friend tonight: the question isn't how much you learned. It's whether you fixed a time.

how: Some Jews keep a set daily study time: a page of Talmud, a chapter of Mishnah, the week's Torah portion, or a short daily study cycle, alone, with a study partner, or by phone with a teacher. Synagogues often hold a short study session between the afternoon and evening prayers.

games.q: what does “ten minutes of learning” mean?
o: a quick quiz to test what you read last week
a long study day kept once a week on Shabbat
a short study time set at the same hour daily

games.q: who said what about study — tap the pairs.
p: did you fix times for Torah?
make your study a fixed thing

s: Jewish study only counts if it fills hours a day
one sage says a chapter morning and evening keeps the verse; another says even the Shema counts.
Hillel says to study once you finally have free time
he says the opposite: don't wait, because the free time may never come.
Rava's question asks whether you fixed times, not how much you learned
the word is kavata, from keva, fixed.

games.q: your friend wants to read the Psalms and plans to start 'when things calm down after finals.' what would Hillel say?
o: fair; study needs a calm mind, so wait for the break.
start now with a small fixed time; the free time may never come.
skip the plan and read whenever the mood strikes.
games.why: Hillel: don't say 'when I have free time I'll study,' maybe you'll never have free time. a small fixed time beats a big someday.

practice: Choose your ten minutes now, and hang them on something that already happens: after coffee, on the bus, before the phone at night. Say the plan to yourself plainly: when this happens, I open the book.
Then decide what you'll read first, so tomorrow begins without deciding.

wordCard.voice: Ten minutes of learning: a short time for study, fixed like an appointment, kept on busy days and thin ones.

orig.note: Hebrew: fixed, set; Shammai's word for study kept at a regular time.

carryVoice: Here's the line: fix a time. The amount can be small; the appointment is real.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (Rava: the questions a person is asked, including 'did you fix times for Torah?')
Mishnah Avot 1:15 (Shammai: make your Torah study fixed)
Mishnah Avot 2:4 (Hillel: do not say 'when I have leisure I will study')
Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 99b (a chapter morning and evening; even the Shema morning and evening)

sources.q: This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth
